rows.searchedFor: if I want the whole company to start using some new app, how do I get that approved?
rows.answer:
The handbook says the process starts with trying the tool, then proposing it, then (once approved) legal and business follow-up.

First, try the tool in a low-risk context where it is easily replaced and doesn't involve sensitive data, checking with #legal first if you're unsure what information can be shared.[1] The goal is to check it works as expected, understand the consequences of introducing it, learn what data it may access, and let others see it in action.[2]

Next, open a pull request in Company Internal and, at the same time, an issue describing why we should adopt the tool. Think about the impact on the whole company, not just your team.[3] The proposal should consider a set of guidelines (not a rigid checklist) so the risks can be weighed holistically against the benefits.[4] Those include:
- Whether other engineers were consulted and relevant teams are supportive.[5]
- Whether security/infra and legal have reviewed it, including whether it would be a subprocessor.[6]
- Whether it affects how sales pitches PostHog or how we communicate with existing customers.[7]
- Whether we could clearly justify to a customer why we use the tool and send data to it.[8]

Many proposals won't make it past this stage, which the handbook says is good.[9]

If approved, the proposer is responsible for coordinating next steps.[10]
- Negotiate business terms with the vendor: cost, licenses or usage limits, contract length, and implementation/onboarding details.[11]
- Once terms are mostly settled, the vendor's documents go through legal review before anything is signed.[12]
- As soon as it looks like you'll move forward, post in #legal that a decision has been made, terms are being negotiated, and contract documents will follow.[13]
- The tool can be used in production once legal review is complete, contracts are signed, and any required subprocessor notice period has passed.[14]

For new subprocessors, customers must get 14 days' notice after the agreement is finalized before the vendor can be used in production.[15]

This process doesn't apply to "cheap decisions" that are easily reversed or only affect your own work; those follow the software guidance on the spending money page.[16]

rows.searchedFor: if my PR touches a github actions workflow, does it need a special reviewer?
rows.answer:
Great care should be taken when writing or modifying a GitHub Actions workflow, since Actions can access (and exfiltrate) secrets scoped to the repo.[1] Workflows are also scanned with Semgrep and CodeQL for common misconfigurations.[1]

Some related points:
- Almost all PRs made to PostHog repositories need a review from another engineer.[2]
- If you need help setting up a new GitHub App for an Action, you can message #team-security.[3]
- In the Shai-Hulud incident, a workflow was changed to check out the PR head commit, so code controlled by the PR author ran in a trusted CI run and could steal the bot token.[4]

rows.searchedFor: is there a rubric or list of criteria I need to hit to move up here?
rows.answer:
Yes, the handbook gives exit criteria for each Salesforce opportunity stage. Bolded exit criteria indicate the minimum standard for the opportunity to advance stages (for typically smaller, more transactional deals).[1] Stages differ by Opportunity Record Type; the following are for the New and Existing Business Record Types[2]:

- Problem Agreement: identified and implicated pain with specific, quantifiable metrics (time/money/risk), and an answer to "What happens if you do nothing?" documented with a real consequence[3]. Also the buyer explicitly said "This is a problem we need to solve" (not just "interesting")[4].
- Solution Agreement: active product usage or a completed POC/trial; a clear, documentable decision made for PostHog; the Economic Buyer identified (name + title); and the Champion identified (name)[5].
- Priority Agreement: budget confirmed; decision process mapped; Economic Buyer said this is a priority (exact quote documented); champion tested; and compelling event known[6].
- Commercial Agreement: price agreed in writing, and all commercial terms agreed (payment terms, contract length, prepaid amount), with the paper process mapped (legal, security, procurement steps + owners + timeline)[7].
- Vendor Approval: contract signed[8].

More detail on each stage's exit criteria is in a spreadsheet the handbook references.[1]

For cross-sells, the stages are different: Discovery, Demo, Trial, and Closed Won (customer paying ≥$100/month on the product)[9]. Not every deal needs every stage.[10]

rows.searchedFor: a customer runs posthog inside their browser extension and their bill is way higher than it should be, how do they fix it?
rows.answer:
The handbook recommends that extension developers persist the ID manually with chrome.storage.local, pass the UUID during posthog.init() with bootstrap.distinctID, call identify() only if the ID has changed, and reduce /flags usage with bootstrap.featureFlags and by disabling polling if needed.[1]

The handbook gives the reason for the inflated bill: Chrome extensions create a new runtime context when waking from idle, and each context re-initialized PostHog without access to prior storage, so a new anonymous distinct_id was created on each wake cycle.[2] Each new ID led to a repeated identify() call, and each identify() call refreshed feature flags.[3]

The steps Wildfire Systems took:
- They persisted a shared UUID via chrome.storage.local, generated once and reused across all extension contexts.[4]
- They passed the distinct_id via bootstrap on every initialization.[5]
- They checked whether the existing distinct_id matched the UUID before calling identify().[6]
- They passed bootstrapped feature flag values during init, reducing the need for real-time flag fetches.[7]
- They used the "My PostHog Billable Usage" dashboard to verify the fixes worked.[8]

One caveat: raising the billing limit mid-cycle did not retroactively unlock flags; only new requests after the monthly reset were allowed.[9]

rows.searchedFor: how do tickets get divvied up on the support team? does everyone work every product?
rows.answer:
Not exactly: technical support engineers split work between shared areas and SME-owned product groups, but nobody is locked into one area.

- All technical support engineers, regardless of SME ownership, work on Analytics products (shared because they make up the highest proportion of tickets) and on unclassified tickets, which should be updated with the correct product group where possible.[1]
- Beyond that, SMEs own specific product groups, with one person from EU and one from NA selected for each group to maintain timezone coverage.[2]
- The handbook lists the product groups as Flags, Data, Replay, Observability + AI & client libraries, and Analytics.[3][4][5][6][7]

Day to day, SMEs start with their SME views, then move to the Technical support shared view, which has all tickets the technical support team is responsible for.[8] They aren't locked into only their SME products: if caught up, they can help with the shared queue, and if swamped, they can ask someone else to help with their SME queue.[9]

When picking tickets, avoid cherry-picking and take the ticket closest to breaching response targets.[10] Also watch whether someone else is already viewing a ticket, to avoid duplicate work.[11]

For new hires, they usually spend the first few weeks focused just on product and web analytics tickets, until they've built more familiarity with the platform as a whole.[12]

rows.searchedFor: what's the cutoff for a new lead to get worked by sales instead of just going self-serve?
rows.answer:
The handbook gives a $20k annual spend threshold: when qualifying a new lead, you consider company size, revenue and funding, i.e. whether they will pay more than $20k for PostHog[1]. Leads below it are covered under "Leads below the sales assist threshold (less than $20K ARR)"[2]. Discovery uses the same line: a qualifier is a path to $2k/mo or $20k/year in spend[3], and having no path to $20k or more in annual spend is a disqualifier[4].

Beyond spend, the handbook lists other factors for deciding between self-serve and hands-on:
- If usage is around 5 million monthly events and 100,000 recordings, they should be hands-on.[5]
- If they want an annual commitment, keep them in the hands-on pipeline.[6]
- If they need help with a guided evaluation and their potential value is high enough, create a Slack Connect channel and keep them in the hands-on pipeline.[6]
- If none of these apply, move them to self-serve.[7]

Qualification also looks at fit and technical capability: qualify if they have the technical capability to succeed, engineers will be involved in the sales process, and there's product/solution fit[8].

rows.searchedFor: I want to interview one of our customers for a story on the website, anyone I should check with before I email them?
rows.answer:
Yes: before reaching out, search for the company in Vitally, and if they already have an assigned Account Executive or CSM, give that person a heads-up, since they might already be working on something with the customer or have extra context on what to ask.[1] If no one is assigned in Vitally, you're clear to reach out directly.[2]

- Some customers have a dedicated Slack channel, which is usually the fastest way to coordinate; otherwise, send an email.[3]
- If you're still looking for the right customer, the handbook suggests starting by asking the PM for that product, since PMs do lots of user interviews and can suggest warm leads.[4]

rows.searchedFor: Do we give customers anything for participating in an interview for a story on the website?
rows.answer:
Yes, the handbook says the last step after the case study is live is a merch credit: once the case study is merged and live on the website, the last step is to send a merch credit to the participants as thank you.[1]

It does not offer discounts in exchange for a case study: we don't offer additional discounts in exchange for a case study, as paying for case studies can devalue them.[2]

rows.answer:
- The benchmark is Culture Amp's 'new tech' companies with fewer than 200 people.[1]
- We take the average score out of 5 and multiply it by 20 to get a % number, which the handbook calls "a bit rough, but close enough" to compare with the benchmark.[1]
- A summary of the results is reported in an Issue, following a template.[2]
